extracted.intended_audience: comedians and readers interested in stand-up and entertainment careers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and informal standards for performing stand-up, developing TV/film projects, touring, and managing creative bandwidth, drawn from an interview with a successful comedian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research new places but don't completely tailor the show
rubrics_metrics.description: "You never want to go into a place completely ignorant, but when I do international shows I try to do the show that I’ve developed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not go into a market completely ignorant — check cultural touchpoints and, for very American references, look for local equivalents. At the same time, avoid over-customizing the show entirely for each market; perform the developed material that hits the notes the audience expects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform the material you've developed (avoid reinventing on arrival)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you’re doing bits where you have references to things that are very American, sometimes you go like, ‘Oh okay, what’s the equivalent here?’ But going in thinking, ‘I’m just gonna do a show that hopefully hits all the notes that these people would want to hear in this market’ – I don’t I don’t do that."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on tested, developed bits for consistency and to reduce risk; minor local adjustments are acceptable, but wholesale rewrites for each venue are discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with anecdotes referencing real people
rubrics_metrics.description: Tom recounts interactions with Chris Tucker and Serena Williams, noting: "She was so unamused and I bombed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes about other celebrities or people can be effective storytelling but may fail if the subject or audience doesn't engage; be prepared for the possibility an anecdote will 'bomb' and have alternative material or responses ready.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live performance gives you control; writing is more vulnerable
rubrics_metrics.description: "When you perform, you’re in control of how the words are said in the cadence, gestures, facial expressions, tone; all of that is your instrument... When you write something, you just hand over pages and you feel very vulnerable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the different skill sets: stage work lets you shape delivery in real time, whereas publishing written material requires surrendering control and accepting greater vulnerability; prepare accordingly when transitioning between mediums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-produce to create opportunities and visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Segura self-produced '69 Minutes', showed it to agents and then Netflix acquired it: "It was kind of an accident that they ended up with it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If traditional channels aren't opening, self-produce work to demonstrate your vision; use finished self-produced projects to pitch agents and platforms — it can catalyze larger distribution deals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value platforms that offer early creative freedom, but expect later scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: On Netflix: "So far, it’s been unreal: 'Go make the show you want to make.' ... it remains to be seen though, they haven’t been given scripts yet so I don’t know what they’re gonna say when they actually read the scripts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appreciate initial hands-off support from platforms, but plan for notes and changes when formal scripts are reviewed; maintain flexibility while maximizing early creative freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: TV and film development is long, arduous, and procedural
rubrics_metrics.description: "Television and film development, that process is always very taxing. It’s long, it’s arduous... you have to remain humble. You have to accept that it is its own process and you have to go through all the steps."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat screen projects as multi-step processes that require patience and adherence to industry procedures; success in stand-up doesn't let you skip development steps for TV/film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage bandwidth; prioritize commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: "You accept that you don’t have the bandwidth to just keep adding things to do... With touring being this aggressive and demanding; when you get back, there’s only so much time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be realistic about how many projects you can sustain alongside heavy touring; selectively add or pause projects (e.g., podcasts) based on available time to avoid burnout and maintain quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touring is aggressive and demanding — plan logistics and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Segura performed 300 shows for 700,000 fans on his last tour and says touring is "aggressive and demanding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect intense schedules and audience volume on major tours; plan rest, recovery, and scheduling to preserve performance quality and personal well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep dreaming and persist toward other creative ambitions
rubrics_metrics.description: "I moved to Los Angeles in 2002 solely because I just wanted to do movies... I’ve just continued to just keep saying it... So I just feel like it’s closer and closer to happening."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain long-term creative goals even if your primary success is in another lane; persistence, continual expression of intent, and incremental steps (writing, collaborating, producing) help move ambitions forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vulnerability and openness as personal and creative growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Segura references a therapist saying he lived in a "narrow emotional bandwidth" and that after injury he became "more expressive" and open to doing things he’d internalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional openness can improve both life and creative work; cultivating expressiveness may broaden material and authenticity on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that not every success transfers automatically to other mediums
rubrics_metrics.description: "I don’t really get to skip any step because I’ve done well in stand up... it’s the same thing for me as anybody else."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand industry gatekeeping: excelling in stand-up doesn't guarantee immediate access to film/TV; follow the same professional steps as others and be prepared to build credentials in each medium.
